_comment: Warehouse queries that feed the ops dashboard, in the order they should run.
These run against the RentViewer data warehouse MCP tool
(mcp__RentViewer_Data_Warehouse__run_query). The warehouse is reachable only
through an authenticated MCP connector, so a plain HTTP job cannot run them --
the refresh is driven by a scheduled Claude session. See docs/ARCHITECTURE.md.
Each entry's `out` is the filename build.py expects under pipeline/raw/.
THE ROSTER IS NOT IN THESE QUERIES. Which communities are reportable comes from
the Property Data Sheet, not the warehouse -- see `reportable_roster` below.
TWO RULES THAT MATTER:
1. Keep `limit` comfortably above the real row count. A pull that hits its
limit is silently truncated -- an early build read $588K of portfolio AR
when the true figure was $1.41M, purely from a 2000-row cap.
2. Never group a snapshot model by both reportMonth and a wide dimension
at once unless you raise the limit to match; the row count multiplies.
If a query times out at 60s, drop a measure or narrow the time range and
re-run rather than lowering the limit.
SPLIT A QUERY THAT TIMES OUT, DO NOT SHRINK IT. Every query here now times
out at 60s with its full measure list -- the warehouse got slower, or the
history got longer. Send the measures in batches of two or three against the
same dimensions and time range, then join the parts on those dimensions.
The parts must agree on row count and key set before they are merged; a
silent mismatch would file a measure against the wrong property-month and
nothing downstream would catch it.
There are eight files here, not six. expense_categories and income_categories
were pulled by hand when the Financials tab was built and never written down,
so refreshes updated financials_by_property_month.json and left the two
category files behind -- they sat at 2,028 rows while financials moved to
2,132. All three share a model and a grain, so their row counts must match.

_comment: The Reportable = Yes roster, and the gate on everything the dashboard shows.
It lives in the `vwr VW_PDS_V2` sheet of the Property Data Sheet on SharePoint,
NOT in the warehouse: the warehouse MCP connector exposes only five models and
VW_PDS_V2 is not among them. If RentViewer ever enables it for AI analysis, this
becomes a seventh query and the SharePoint read goes away.
Read the newest file under the SharePoint path below with the Microsoft 365
connector, take the `vwr VW_PDS_V2` sheet, keep rows where Reportable is exactly
Yes (blank and No are both excluded), and write one JSON object per row with the
fields listed in `fields`. The warehouse joins on `property_name` exactly.
Refuse to build if this file is missing or empty rather than falling back to a
heuristic roster: guessing which of ~150 propertyName values are real communities
is exactly what this file exists to prevent.
READER TRUNCATION WILL SILENTLY DROP COMMUNITIES. The workbook has six
worksheets and the resource reader caps at roughly 200KB, so a read of
`vwr VW_PDS_V2` came back with 203 of its 237 rows and the note '[Output
truncated -- 32 more rows in this sheet ... not shown]' buried mid-file.
Parsed as if complete it yielded 46 Reportable = Yes instead of 66, dropped
22 live communities including Great Oak, Riverwalk, The Oaks and Windward
Knoll, and resurrected Cambridge and Geiger which Austin had removed by hand.
So: after any read, CHECK FOR THE TRUNCATION NOTE and check the row count
against the `NNN rows x NN columns` figure in the sheet heading. If they
disagree, the read is partial and must not be written. Same failure mode as
the row-limit warning on the queries below, different mechanism.
When a read is partial and the workbook's lastModifiedDateTime is unchanged
since the roster was last built, the roster is already current and the right
move is to leave it alone and say so, not to rewrite it from the fragment.
reportable_roster._fields_note: Extended past the original eleven when the hot sheet landed: it needs Total Core Units as its occupancy denominator, Purchase Date and Price, POH for the PDS-vs-asset-listing check, and the two lot rents. Total Core Units lives on the PDS Clean sheet rather than VW_PDS_V2.

_comment: The eviction tracker, and the only source that can say which receivables are
already in eviction. Without it the 90+ bucket is one undifferentiated number.
It is a scripted Rent Manager report, not an API report and not a warehouse
model, so it cannot be pulled with run_report. It lands on SharePoint daily.
READ THE UNDATED FILE at `sharepoint_file`. A dated copy is archived into
`Historical Eviction Tracker/`, but that folder runs a day or two behind the
live one -- an earlier build looked only there, saw nothing past Aug 31, and
wrongly concluded the daily job had stopped.
Pipe the connector's output straight into the staging script, which strips the
resident name and case number and normalises the dates:
python3 pipeline/stage_eviction.py <downloaded-or-mcp-output>
Never write this file by hand and never stage it without that script. It is the
only raw source that arrives with resident names attached, and the standalone
build gets emailed around.
The build survives without it: the in-eviction bucket simply empties and every
balance falls through to needs-action. So check the as-of date in the output --
build.py raises a flag once it is more than two days old.
eviction_tracker.join_on: ShortName plus Name (the unit), against EntitiesShortName plus SubEntitiesName on the AR detail

remove a dimension between batches; the merge keys on them and will refuse.

_comment: REPLACES the Rent Manager API call (report 244). Austin's call: read the
SharePoint drop instead. It is strictly better and it already has history.
A dated CSV lands here every morning around 08:02-08:09 ET. 387 files as of
2026-09-08, so months of daily home-level history already exist -- assets are
the one thing we do NOT have to start accumulating from today.
125 columns against the API's 30. What the API never gave us:
* the entire home setup sequence with dates -- permit submitted/received,
demo, footers/pads, spot units, set-side-tie-down, interior trim out,
water/sewer/electrical/AC connection, skirting/gutter, steps/deck,
PUNCH OUT, cert of occupancy. Twelve stages, each with a date, which
makes time-in-stage derivable per home right now off existing files.
* `UDF: Punch Out Date`. The dashboard carries a note saying there is no
punch stage in Rent Manager. There is; it was never in the API pull.
* Market Rent, Occupant, Est. Rehab Cost/Demo, the title workflow, and the
lease-option (LOP) terms.
TWO HAZARDS BEFORE USING THE HISTORY:
1. The schema is not stable across the archive. Files around 2026-08-13
to 08-17 and 08-31 carry a different header that begins with property
name and short code ("Whispering Pines FL","WPMH",...) rather than the
125-column layout below. Read the header of every file; never assume
column positions across dates.
2. Column 101 is `UDF: Sewer Connection Date'` with a trailing apostrophe
in the source. Match on the exact string or normalise it.

_comment: Austin is enabling a warehouse view. Until then there is no daily prospect
feed, so stage history still has to be accumulated forward. Three one-off
exports exist on SharePoint and none of them repeats:
1. `.../SAM Umbrella/initial info/AB reports sent/JW Claude_*-1-Prospect
Stage Listing.csv` -- Rent Manager report 676. Columns: Stage, Name,
Property, Unit, First Contact, Last Contact, Stage Date. This is the
shape we want; it is a single snapshot from 2026-05-21.
2. `.../SAM Umbrella/initial info/DW_Prospect Status Report_*.csv` -- the
`DW_` prefix suggests this is already a warehouse export. Carries
ProspectStage plus `Days In System` and `Application Days`, i.e.
time-in-stage precomputed. Closest match to what Austin described.
3. `.../SAM CRM & Prospect Reporting/Prospects_YYYY_MM_DD.csv` -- Zoho CRM
export. Prospect Owner, Prospect Source, Prospect Status.
PII. Files 1 and 3 carry prospect names, and the Zoho export also carries
email addresses and phone numbers. Any of these must be staged through the
same discipline as the eviction tracker: strip the identifying columns and
refuse to write a file that still contains them. Keep Property and Unit as
the join key. See pipeline/stage_eviction.py for the pattern.
